title: Allies of World War I
description: Military coalition in World War I
wiki_lead:
The Allies or the Entente (UK: , US:  on-TONT) was an international military coalition of countries led by the French Republic, the United Kingdom, the Russian Empire, the United States, the Kingdom of Italy, and the Empire of Japan against the Central Powers of the German Empire, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, and the Tsardom of Bulgaria in World War I (1914–1918).
By the end of the first decade of the 20th century, the major European powers were divided between the Triple Entente and the Triple Alliance. The Triple Entente was made up of the United Kingdom, France, and Russia. The Triple Alliance was originally composed of Germany, Austria–Hungary, and Italy, but Italy remained neutral in 1914. As the war progressed, each coalition added new members. Japan joined the Entente in 1914 and, despite proclaiming its neutrality at the beginning of the war, Italy also joined the Entente in 1915. The term "Allies" became more widely used than "Entente", although the United Kingdom, France, Russia, and Italy were also referred to as the Quadruple Entente and, together with Japan, as the Quintuple Entente. The five British Dominions (the Commonwealth of Australia, the Dominion of Canada, the Dominion of New Zealand, the Dominion of Newfoundland, and the Union of South Africa) all fought alongside the British. The colonies of Allied countries, such as the American Philippines, Belgian Congo, British India, French Algeria, and Japanese Korea, were also used as a source of manpower by the colonial powers.
The United States joined near the end of the war in 1917 (the same year in which Russia withdrew from the conflict) as an "associated power" rather than an official ally. Primary reasons for why the United States joined the war include the unrestricted submarine warfare waged by Germany in the Atlantic, the revelation of the Zimmermann telegram, and strong economic and political ties with the Allies. Other "associated members" of the Allies included Serbia, Belgium, Montenegro, Asir, Nejd and Hasa, Portugal, Romania, Hejaz, Panama, Cuba, Greece, China, Siam, Brazil, Armenia, Luxembourg, Guatemala, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, Haiti, Liberia, and Honduras. The treaties signed at the Paris Peace Conference recognised the British Empire, France, Italy, Japan, and the United States as "the Principal Allied and Associated Powers"; France, the UK, Italy, and the US were also referred as the "Big Four" top powers of the war.

Background
When the war began in 1914, the Central Powers were opposed by the Triple Entente, formed in 1907 when the agreement between the United Kingdom and Russia complemented existing agreements between the three powers.
Fighting commenced when Austria invaded Serbia on 28 July 1914, in response to the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to Emperor Franz Joseph I; this brought Serbia's ally Montenegro into the war on 9 August and it attacked the Austrian naval base at Cattaro, modern Kotor. grok_lead: The Allies of World War I, also designated the Entente Powers, constituted a coalition of nations that opposed the Central Powers âprimarily Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, and Bulgaria âthroughout the global conflict from 1914 to 1918. The core of this alliance originated from the Triple Entente, formalized by agreements among France, the United Kingdom, and the Russian Empire prior to the war's outbreak, which committed these powers to mutual support against aggression. Initially including smaller states such as Serbia, Belgium, and Montenegro, the coalition expanded significantly with the entry of Japan in 1914, Italy in 1915 following its defection from the Triple Alliance, and the United States in 1917, alongside contributions from British dominions like Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and South Africa, as well as colonial forces from India and elsewhere. This diverse assembly leveraged superior industrial capacity, naval dominanceâexemplified by the British Royal Navy's blockadeâand eventually overwhelming manpower to prevail, culminating in the Armistice of 11 November 1918 that ended hostilities. The Allies' victory, achieved at the cost of approximately 6 million military deaths and profound societal disruptions, dismantled the Central Powers ' empires and imposed punitive terms via the Treaty of Versailles, though internal frictions, such as Russia's 1917 withdrawal following the Bolshevik Revolution and debates over unified command, tested the coalition's cohesion. Strategic coordination improved with bodies like the Supreme War Council established in 1917, enabling decisive offensives in 1918 that exploited German exhaustion. Defining characteristics included the mobilization of imperial resources, with over 2.5 million troops from the British Empire alone, underscoring the war's imperial dimensions and the Allies' reliance on global logistics for sustenance.
